description: The Sangha and Three Jewels; monastic and lay life; Ten Precepts; Wesak, Vassa and major festivals.
content_html:
The Three Jewels

When Buddhists convert or reaffirm their commitment to their tradition, they recite the Three Refuges: “I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dhamma, I take refuge in the Sangha.” These three — the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha — are known collectively as the Three Jewels (Tiratana). Each represents an indispensable element: the Buddha is the teacher who discovered the path; the Dhamma is the truth he taught; and the Sangha is the community that preserves and practises those teachings. Without all three, the Buddhist path cannot function.

The Monastic Sangha

The monastic sangha consists of fully ordained monks (bhikkhus) and nuns (bhikkhunis). Monks and nuns take the Ten Precepts, which are a stricter set of ethical rules than the Five Precepts observed by lay Buddhists. The Ten Precepts include the Five Precepts plus additional rules: not eating after midday, not attending entertainment, not using garlands or perfumes, not using a high bed, and not handling money. Monastics depend on the lay community for food, offered each morning on the alms round. In return, they preserve the Dhamma through study, teaching and practice.

Key Fact

The Ten Precepts observed by Buddhist monks and nuns include the Five Precepts (not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not lying, not taking intoxicants) plus five additional rules, including not eating after midday, not attending entertainment and not handling money. This stricter code enables full-time devoted practice.

Ordination of Women

The ordination of women into the full bhikkhuni (nun) sangha has a complex history. According to tradition, the Buddha’s stepmother Mahapajapati Gotami was the first woman to be ordained, after persistent requests. However, the bhikkhuni lineage died out in Theravada communities and was not revived for many centuries. Today, the issue of full ordination for women remains contested: in some Theravada countries (notably Thailand and Burma), full ordination for women is not officially permitted by the monks’ sangha. In Mahayana traditions, full ordination for women has been maintained. The Dhammapada 360–369 praises the qualities of a well-restrained monastic, regardless of gender, and contemporary advocates for women’s ordination appeal to the Buddha’s original decision to ordain Mahapajapati Gotami.

The Lay Sangha

The lay sangha comprises all Buddhists who have not taken full monastic ordination. Lay Buddhists observe the Five Precepts, support the monastic community through dana (giving), attend temple on Uposatha days, perform puja at home shrines and study the Dhamma. The relationship between monks/nuns and lay Buddhists is one of mutual support: monastics provide teaching and spiritual merit; lay people provide material support. This interdependence has sustained Buddhism across many countries for over 2,500 years.

The monastic code (Vinaya) contains detailed rules governing every aspect of monastic life — from how robes are worn to how disputes within the community are resolved. Monks and nuns live according to these rules in a vihara or gompa. Daily life typically includes early morning meditation, the alms round (in Theravada countries), communal chanting, study of the Dhamma and evening meditation. Monasteries serve the surrounding lay community as centres of teaching, ceremony and social support.

Major Buddhist Festivals

Buddhist festivals mark key events in the Buddha’s life and the rhythms of the monastic calendar. Their observance varies significantly between Theravada, Mahayana and Tibetan traditions.

Key Fact

Wesak (also called Vaisakha or Vesak) is the most widely celebrated Buddhist festival. In Theravada Buddhism, it falls on the full moon of the lunar month of Vesakha and commemorates three key events in the Buddha’s life: his birth, his enlightenment and his Parinibbana (final passing). In Mahayana traditions, especially in Japan, these events are celebrated separately. The birth of the Buddha is celebrated as Hanamatsuri (the Flower Festival) on 8 April, when a statue of the baby Buddha is bathed in sweet tea to recall the legend that the gods showered him with flower petals at birth.

Vassa (the Rain Retreat) is a Theravada festival running for approximately three months during the monsoon season. During Vassa, monks must remain within their monastery, using the time for intensive meditation and study. Lay Buddhists support the monastery with additional offerings and often take on additional precepts during this period. Vassa ends with the festival of Kathina, when lay people offer robes and supplies to the monastic community.

Uposatha Days occur four times a month in Theravada Buddhism, aligned with the phases of the moon. On Uposatha days, lay Buddhists visit the temple, observe eight precepts rather than five, listen to Dhamma teachings and meditate with the monastic community. These days function as regular “Sabbath-style” occasions for deepened practice.

Parinirvana Day is observed in Mahayana Buddhist traditions on 15 February. It commemorates the death (final Parinirvana) of the Buddha at the age of 80, after which he entered the state of complete nirvana, beyond all rebirth. Buddhists reflect on their own impermanence and the importance of practising the Dhamma while they still can.

Lama Tsong Khapa Day (Ganden Ngamchoe) is a Tibetan Buddhist festival commemorating Lama Tsong Khapa (1357–1419 CE), the founder of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, which includes the Dalai Lamas. It is celebrated on the 25th day of the 10th Tibetan month by lighting butter lamps and offering prayers. This festival illustrates an important principle: Buddhist festivals are not limited to events in the life of the historical Buddha, but may honour great teachers and bodhisattvas within a particular tradition. The influence of local culture is strong — Tibetan Buddhism’s festival calendar reflects indigenous Himalayan customs alongside Buddhist doctrine.
exam_tip_html: A very common error is confusing the Three Jewels with the Three Marks of Existence — they are completely different: the Three Jewels are Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha; the Three Marks are anicca, dukkha and anatta. When answering an “Explain” question (6 marks) on festivals, always name the festival, state what it commemorates and explain why it matters to Buddhists. For a 15-mark Discuss, you can contrast Theravada and Mahayana treatments of the same event (for example, Wesak vs Hanamatsuri) as two valid perspectives. Accurate spelling of Sangha, Wesak, Vipassana and Vassa is rewarded in extended responses.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Sangha is one of the Three Jewels (Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha) and comprises the monastic sangha (monks and nuns who observe the Ten Precepts) and the lay sangha (householders who observe the Five Precepts). Mutual support between both sustains Buddhism.
  • Wesak is the most important Buddhist festival, marking the Buddha’s birth, enlightenment and Parinibbana; in Mahayana Japan, the birth is separately celebrated as Hanamatsuri. Vassa is the Theravada rains retreat and Uposatha days are regular occasions for lay practice.
  • Buddhist festivals vary between Theravada, Mahayana and Tibetan traditions, reflecting the Buddha’s life and great teachers; local culture shapes how they are observed, as seen in Lama Tsong Khapa Day in Tibetan Buddhism.

practice_questions.text: State one festival celebrated by Theravada Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any one of: Wesak / Vassa / Uposatha Days / Kathina. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the lay sangha in Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: The lay sangha are Buddhists who live as householders rather than monastics [1]; they observe the Five Precepts, support monks and nuns through offerings (dana), perform puja and attend festivals [1]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the significance of Wesak for Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: Wesak commemorates the three most important events in the Buddha's life — his birth, enlightenment and Parinibbana [1]; it is the most widely celebrated Buddhist festival, observed across Theravada and Mahayana traditions [1]; Buddhists mark it with offerings, meditation, chanting and acts of generosity, renewing their commitment to the Buddhist path [1]. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the Sangha is important to Buddhists.
Refer to Buddhist teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Sangha is one of the Three Jewels — without the community of practitioners, the Dhamma cannot be preserved and transmitted. Taking refuge in the Sangha (the Three Refuges) is a foundational act of Buddhist commitment.
• The monastic sangha provides teaching, preserves the Vinaya and Dhamma, and offers a model of dedicated practice. The Dhammapada 360–369 praises the qualities of a well-restrained monastic, showing the spiritual authority the Sangha holds.
• The Sangha provides lay Buddhists with a community for festival observance, Uposatha days and support — reducing isolation and fostering collective commitment to the path.
[6 marks — 3 marks per reason: 1 simple point, 2 developed, 3 with teaching/source]

practice_questions.text: 'The monastic sangha is more important to Buddhism than the lay sangha.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The monastic sangha preserves the Vinaya and Dhamma, trains future teachers and provides the model of full-time dedicated practice; without it, Buddhist teachings would be lost.
• Monks and nuns observe the Ten Precepts, living a life of greater renunciation than lay Buddhists, which is traditionally seen as generating greater spiritual progress and merit.
• The Buddha himself was a monastic who modelled renunciation; the Sangha he established began with monks (the first five disciples at Sarnath), not householders.

Arguments against:
• The lay sangha sustains the monastic community materially through alms, offerings and donations; without lay support, monasteries cannot function.
• The Dhammapada 360–369 praises restraint without limiting this to monastics; in Mahayana traditions, dedicated lay practitioners (such as the famous layman Vimalakirti) are considered equally capable of achieving high spiritual attainment.
• In contemporary Western Buddhism, lay-led communities are numerically dominant; defining the lay sangha as secondary marginalises the majority of Buddhists.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources and Theravada/Mahayana contrast; weighing and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides presented with some Buddhist teaching; conclusion reached.
Developing: One side stronger; limited teaching reference.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; little Buddhist content. [15 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the importance of Vassa (the Rain Retreat) for Theravada Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: Vassa is a three-month rains retreat during which Theravada monks must remain in their monastery [1]; it is a period of intensive meditation and Dhamma study, allowing monastics to deepen their practice away from travel [1]; lay Buddhists increase their support through additional offerings and may observe extra precepts, strengthening the bond between monastic and lay communities [1]. [3 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Buddhist monks and nuns observe the _____ Precepts, which are stricter than the five observed by lay Buddhists.
_____ is the three-month Theravada rains retreat during which monks remain in their monastery.
Match each festival to its tradition and significance:
right: Theravada and Mahayana festival marking the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death
Tibetan Buddhist festival honouring the founder of the Gelug school
Moon-phase observance days for Theravada lay Buddhists to deepen practice

flashcard_questions.q: What are the Three Jewels (Tiratana) of Buddhism?
flashcard_questions.a: The Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha.
The community of ordained monks (bhikkhus) and nuns (bhikkhunis) who practise full-time.

flashcard_questions.q: What additional rules do the Ten Precepts add beyond the Five Precepts?
flashcard_questions.a: Not eating after midday, not attending entertainment, not using garlands or perfumes, not using a high bed, not handling money.

flashcard_questions.q: What three events does Wesak commemorate?
flashcard_questions.a: The Buddha's birth, his enlightenment and his Parinibbana (final passing).
A Mahayana Japanese festival (Flower Festival) celebrating the Buddha's birth on 8 April.
The three-month Theravada rains retreat during which monks remain in their monastery.
Four monthly Theravada observance days when lay Buddhists visit the temple and keep eight precepts.
The death of the Buddha at the age of 80 and his final entry into complete nirvana.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was Lama Tsong Khapa and why is his day important?
flashcard_questions.a: He founded the Tibetan Gelug school (1357–1419); his day is marked with butter lamps and prayers.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the lay sangha support the monastic sangha?
flashcard_questions.a: Through dana — giving food, robes and offerings during the alms round and festivals.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the ordination of women into the bhikkhuni sangha contested in some Theravada countries?
flashcard_questions.a: The bhikkhuni lineage died out and has not been officially reinstated in countries like Thailand.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Dhammapada verses praise the qualities of a well-restrained monastic?

glossary_terms.definition: The Buddhist community of monks, nuns and lay practitioners; one of the Three Jewels at the heart of Buddhist life.
The Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, regarded as the three most precious things in Buddhism.
The community of ordained monks (bhikkhus) and nuns (bhikkhunis) who have left household life to practise full-time.
The community of Buddhist practitioners who live in the world as householders, rather than as ordained monks or nuns.
The most important Theravada Buddhist festival, marking the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and Parinibbana on the full moon of Vesakha.
The three-month Theravada Buddhist rains retreat, during which monks remain in their monastery and intensify their practice.
